claims.text: Equiatomic FeCoNi has an FCC structure, high saturation magnetization, and a low coercive field.
Introducing Cr into FeCoNi will increase coercivity relative to FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt.
An equiatomic FeCoNiCr composition has configurational entropy greater than 1.0R.
FeCoNiCr can be processed as a homogeneous, single-phase FCC solid solution.
Cr incorporation into FeCoNi increases local lattice distortion.
Cr incorporation into FeCoNi promotes competing antiferromagnetic interactions.
Cr-induced lattice distortion and antiferromagnetic interactions act as domain-wall pinning sites.
Cr increases chemical heterogeneity in the FCC FeCoNi matrix.
Cr-induced antiferromagnetic coupling and chemical heterogeneity hinder domain-wall motion.
Replacing ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr increased coercivity in an earlier related high-entropy alloy.
FeCoNiCr will have a higher coercive field than the cited soft-ferromagnetic FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt derivatives.
Adding Cr to FeCoNi may moderately reduce saturation magnetization.
FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt are soft ferromagnets with low coercivity.
Cr addition or unsuitable annealing can promote secondary-phase formation.
Secondary phases could negate the proposed coercivity increase.
Excessive Cr or improper processing may form brittle intermetallic compounds.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as selectively replacing part of Co with Cr, but the example equiatomic FeCoNiCr composition is a four-component equiatomic addition that lowers the atomic fractions of Fe, Co, and Ni equally rather than selectively replacing Co.

The boundary limits the hypothesis to single-phase material without decomposition, whereas the falsification rule treats detection of secondary phases as falsification. Such a sample would instead fall outside the stated applicability conditions and would not decisively test the bounded hypothesis.
